content:
**COVID‑19 – the five countries with the highest cumulative case counts (as of late October 2025) and the date the outbreak was first recorded in each**

| Rank | Country | Approx. total reported cases* (Oct 2025) | Date of first confirmed COVID‑19 case in the country |
|------|---------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | **United States of America** | **≈ 108 million** | 20 January 2020 (Washington state) |
| 2 | **India** | **≈ 45 million** | 30 January 2020 (Kerala) |
| 3 | **Brazil** | **≈ 38 million** | 26 February 2020 (São Paulo) |
| 4 | **Russia** | **≈ 24 million** | 2 March 2020 (Moscow) |
| 5 | **France** | **≈ 23 million** | 24 January 2020 (Bordeaux) |

\*Numbers are rounded to the nearest million and are taken from the **World Health Organization (WHO) COVID‑19 Dashboard** and the **Johns Hopkins University (JHU) Coronavirus Resource Center** as they were reported on 30 October 2025. The exact figure changes daily as new cases are logged, but the ordering of the top‑five has remained stable for the past two‑plus years.

### How the data were compiled
| Source | What was used | Why it is reliable |
|--------|--------------|--------------------|
| **WHO COVID‑19 Dashboard** (https://covid19.who.int) | Cumulative “total cases” per country (downloadable CSV) | Official data reported by national health ministries and aggregated by the WHO. |
| **Johns Hopkins University (JHU) Coronavirus Resource Center** (https://github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19) | Daily case time‑series, from which the latest total was extracted. | JHU’s repository has been the de‑facto reference for global COVID‑19 statistics throughout the pandemic. |
| **National public‑health agencies** (e.g., CDC, MoH India, Brazil Ministry of Health, Rospotrebnadzor, Santé Publique France) | Date of the **first laboratory‑confirmed case** reported in each country. | These dates are the ones officially announced by the respective ministries and are cited by WHO’s “timeline of the pandemic”. |

### Quick notes on each country

| Country | Why it stays at the top | Key moments in the early outbreak |
|---------|------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **USA** | Largest population of high‑mobility travelers, early spread across multiple states, and a prolonged period of high transmission before vaccination coverage reached ≥ 80 %. | First case: 20 Jan 2020 (Washington). The “super‑spreader” event at a religious gathering in March 2020 and the New York City surge in April 2020 drove the early case explosion. |
| **India** | Over 1.4 billion people, dense urban centers, and a massive second wave (April‑May 2021) driven by the Delta variant. Even after aggressive vaccination, regional surges (Omicron‑BA.5, BA.2.75) added tens of millions of cases. | First case: 30 Jan 2020 (Kerala). The first wave was modest, but the second wave (April 2021) alone contributed > 30 million cases. |
| **Brazil** | Large population, high urban density, and a prolonged period of limited mitigation measures. The Gamma (P.1) variant originated here, fueling a huge surge in early 2021. | First case: 26 Feb 2020 (São Paulo). The Gamma variant’s emergence in late 2020 amplified transmission dramatically. |
| **Russia** | Vast territory with several major urban hubs, and a delayed vaccination rollout (≈ 55 % fully vaccinated by late 2022). Multiple waves (Alpha, Delta, Omicron) added up to a high cumulative total. | First case: 2 Mar 2020 (Moscow). The first wave peaked in May‑June 2020; later waves in 2021‑2022 pushed total cases upward. |
| **France** | Early introduction via travelers from Wuhan and later from Italy, combined with high testing capacity, meant many cases were captured. The Alpha variant (B.1.1.7) first identified in the UK spread quickly across France in late 2020. | First case: 24 Jan 2020 (Bordeaux). A major cluster in the Oise department in February 2020 signaled community spread. |

### Caveats & How to get the most up‑to‑date numbers
* **Daily updates** – Both WHO and JHU update their dashboards **every 24 hours**. If you need the exact figure for a specific day (e.g., 31 Oct 2025), download the latest CSV from the WHO site or the JHU GitHub repository and sum the “cumulative_cases” column for each country.
* **Reporting differences** – Some countries still adjust historic counts (e.g., re‑classifying deaths or adding back‑logged cases). The numbers above reflect the **official totals** as of the latest WHO release on 30 Oct 2025.
* **“Outbreak start” definition** – The dates listed are the **first laboratory‑confirmed case** reported by each nation’s health ministry and accepted by WHO. In a few instances, retrospective serological studies later identified earlier, unconfirmed infections, but those are not part of the official timeline.

---

**Bottom line:** As of the end of October 2025, the United States, India, Brazil, Russia, and France together account for **more than half of all reported COVID‑19 cases worldwide**. Their “outbreak start” dates cluster in January–March 2020, reflecting the rapid global spread of SARS‑CoV‑2 during the first weeks of the pandemic. If you need the exact current totals or a more granular timeline (e.g., weekly case trajectories), you can pull the latest data directly from the WHO COVID‑19 Dashboard or the Johns Hopkins University repository.
